items.stimulus: Stainless steel is often thought to resist rust because it is especially hard. In fact, its rust resistance comes from chromium: steel that contains at least 10 percent chromium forms a thin oxide film on its surface, and that film blocks rust. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: forms a thin oxide film that blocks rust.
resists rust mainly because it is very hard.
resists rust better than every other steel alloy.
was designed to be used in the hulls of ships.
items.explanation: This is the most basic version of the 'link the two facts' inference. Fact 1 says that steel with at least 10 percent chromium forms an oxide film that blocks rust. Fact 2 says the new alloy is a steel with 12 percent chromium. The shared term is 'at least 10 percent chromium', and 12 percent meets it. Cut that term out and you get A → C: the new alloy forms the rust-blocking film. Choice A states exactly that link and adds nothing. Harder inference questions ask for the same move inside longer, denser passages, usually after the words 'taken together' or 'therefore'.

per_choice.A: You read leaving the main sequence as a sign of age. Stars in a cluster are the same age, and cluster M is the younger one, so R is younger than P.
per_choice.C: You reversed the chain, maybe because P belongs to the older cluster. A star that is still on the main sequence in an older cluster has to be lighter than one that has left it in a younger cluster.
per_choice.D: You stretched one comparison to a whole cluster. Stars still on M's main sequence can be any small mass, so 'every' is not established.

items.stimulus: Iron from plant foods is poorly absorbed, but vitamin C eaten in the same meal raises how much of it the body takes up. Tea is often blamed for lowering iron absorption. However, nutrition researcher Priya Raman found that tea's polyphenols reduce absorption of plant iron only when the tea is drunk within an hour of the meal. In her trial, participants ate a lentil meal with orange juice, which is rich in vitamin C, and drank black tea two hours later. Compared with the same meal eaten with water and no tea, their absorption of the lentils' iron would be expected to be ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: about the same, because the tea would cancel the boost from the juice.
lower, because tea polyphenols reduce the absorption of plant iron.
higher, because the tea came too late to offset the juice's boost.
higher, because tea taken after a meal also aids iron absorption.
items.explanation: The juice supplies vitamin C with the meal, so absorption goes up. The tea's polyphenols matter only within an hour, and this tea came two hours later, so it removes nothing. The net result is higher absorption than the plain meal.

A.why: You saw both effects and let them cancel out. You missed the time limit: tea two hours later is outside the one-hour window, so it offsets nothing.

B.why: You used only the popular view that tea lowers iron absorption. Raman's finding limits that effect to tea taken within an hour, and you also left out the juice.

D.why: You got the direction right but gave a reason nobody stated. The passage says late tea fails to lower absorption, not that it raises it.
